description.sr_latin: Kako da zvučiš kao da si odrastao u Srbiji — ili bar da nasmešiš ekipu.
description.en: How to sound like you grew up in Serbia — or at least make the crew laugh.

phrases.context: You're bursting to share juicy gossip — open the story to your friend before the details.
phrases.notes: 'Brate' = vocative of 'brat' (brother), but it's a filler said to anyone — even women use it.

phrases.sr_latin: Brate moj, šta da ti kažem.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Брате мој, шта да ти кажем.
phrases.en: My brother, what can I tell you.
phrases.context: Your friend asks how you're holding up after a rough week — sigh out a resigned non-answer.
phrases.notes: 'Šta da ti kažem' = 'what should I tell you' (da + present) — a verbal shrug, not a real question.

phrases.context: Your friend lays out their troubles and you feel for them but can't fix any of it — sigh.
phrases.notes: The opening 'e' adds a wistful, philosophical weight — the tone of someone who's seen it all.

phrases.context: Your best friend walks in and you greet him with a big, warm, folksy welcome.
phrases.notes: 'Bajo' = an affectionate term for a man, common in Bosnia and western Serbia — folksy and warm.

phrases.context: Your buddy makes a ridiculous claim — playfully shoo him away like you don't believe a word.
phrases.notes: Clipped from 'marš' (march off!). Sharp and iconic — softened to teasing among friends by tone.

phrases.context: Your friend tells you something hard to believe and you wave it off with a grinning dismissal.
phrases.notes: 'Idi' = go (imperative). 'Bre' has no translation — it just adds heat. 'Bre' came in from Turkish.

phrases.context: Your friend does something silly and you ruffle his hair and call him a name with a grin.
phrases.notes: 'Budala' is grammatically feminine even aimed at a man, so 'jedna' agrees. 'Budala' came from Turkish.

phrases.en: Don't be annoying. / Stop being a pain.
phrases.context: Your friend keeps nagging you about the same thing — tell him to quit being a pain.
phrases.notes: 'Nemoj da' + present = 'don't' (negative imperative). 'Smarati' = to bore/annoy — peak teen slang.

phrases.en: Where you at, man? / What's up?
phrases.context: You spot a buddy across the street and call out an extra-relaxed, slangy hello.
phrases.notes: 'De' is clipped from 'gde' (where) — the dropped 'g' is what makes it sound street and casual.

phrases.context: You greet a close friend and pile on a little extra warmth for good measure.
phrases.notes: 'Ćao' came from Italian 'ciao'. Tacking 'bre' on the end makes the hello unmistakably Serbian.

phrases.context: Your friend keeps stewing over something small — tell him to let the whole thing go.
phrases.notes: 'Pusti' = let go (imperative). The lead-in 'ma' adds a dismissive 'oh, come on' shrug.

phrases.context: A friend apologizes for forgetting to call back — brush it off, it's totally fine.
phrases.notes: Literally 'there's no connection' — 'nema' forces 'veza' into the genitive 'veze'.

phrases.context: Your friend says something so funny you can barely breathe — react to the joke.
phrases.notes: 'Od' (from) takes the genitive 'smeha'. Swap in 'gladi' (hunger) or 'dosade' (boredom) the same way.

phrases.en: I'm done. / I'm spent. / I cracked.
phrases.context: You're wrung out after a brutal day or laughing too hard — say you've got nothing left.
phrases.notes: Literally 'I burst' (past tense, masculine 'pukao'). A woman says 'Pukla sam'.

phrases.en: This is madness. / This is a madhouse.
phrases.context: You're stuck in chaotic gridlocked traffic — sum up the scene in one exasperated line.
phrases.notes: 'Ludnica' = madhouse/asylum, from 'lud' (crazy). Used for any scene of happy or stressful chaos.

phrases.context: You just did something genuinely dumb and you own it out loud to your friend.
phrases.notes: Calling yourself a 'majmun' (monkey) is gentle self-mockery. 'Majmun' came in from Turkish.

phrases.context: You mess up in a way that's so completely on-brand for you that it's almost funny.
phrases.notes: 'Klasičan' = classic/typical (masculine). A woman says 'Klasična ja'.

phrases.context: You did something cringeworthy in public and you're confessing it with a resigned sigh.
phrases.notes: 'Obrukati se' = to make a fool of yourself (reflexive 'se'); past 'obrukao' is masculine.

phrases.context: Some tiny inconvenience lands on you and you throw your hands up in theatrical self-pity.
phrases.notes: Played for laughs over trivial things — the bigger the drama over the smaller the problem, the better.

phrases.context: Another small thing goes wrong for you and you're sure the universe has a personal grudge.
phrases.notes: 'Meni' = to me (dative), the one experiencing it. 'Dešavati se' = to happen (reflexive 'se').

phrases.en: What kind of life is this, bro.
phrases.context: One more thing goes sideways and you let out a half-joking lament about your whole existence.
phrases.notes: 'Koji' = what/which here. Usually hilariously overdramatic rather than genuinely bleak.

phrases.context: You miss the bus or your phone dies and you declare total catastrophe over the minor setback.
phrases.notes: Literally 'I've fallen through' (past, masculine 'propao'). A woman says 'Propala sam'.

phrases.sr_latin: Smešno mi je što je tužno.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Смешно ми је што је тужно.
phrases.context: Your friend shares a depressing-but-relatable observation and you laugh at exactly how true it is.
phrases.notes: 'Smešno mi je' = it's funny to me (dative 'mi'). 'Što' = because here — the heart of Balkan dark humor.

phrases.context: You and your friend are about to do something pointless or reckless — rally him to commit anyway.
phrases.notes: 'Će' is the future clitic of 'hteti', here standing in for the verb. An ironic rallying cry.

phrases.context: You clearly have a strong opinion but saying it out loud would only cause trouble right now.
phrases.notes: 'Ćutati' = to keep quiet; 'ćutim' = I stay silent (present). Saying it loudly is, of course, the joke.

phrases.context: A plan keeps falling apart and you're done with it — tell your friend to drop the whole thing.
phrases.notes: 'Terati' = to drive/push; 'teraj to' literally 'drive that off'. A milder cousin of cruder versions.

phrases.context: A friend asks how things are going — answer in one laid-back word that it's all relaxed.
phrases.notes: Literally 'lightly', from 'lak' (light/easy). The Serbian 'easy-peasy', used for taking it slow.

phrases.context: Your friend is rushing around stressed — tell him to slow down, life isn't a race.
phrases.notes: 'Žuriš' = you're rushing (present). 'Polako' (slowly/easy) is a core Balkan value: rushing is suspect.

phrases.context: Your friend is panicking about a small problem — reassure him there's nothing to stress about.
phrases.notes: 'Nema' forces 'frka' (panic/stress) into the genitive 'frke'. Very common among younger speakers.

phrases.context: You stub your toe on the table leg — let out the natural little cry.
phrases.notes: The all-purpose Serbian exclamation — pain, surprise, pity, delight. You'll hear it constantly.

phrases.context: You're nudging your friend to get moving, or wrapping up a chat — toss out the all-purpose nudge.
phrases.notes: 'Ajde' = let's/come on. Flips by tone: encouragement, impatience, agreement, even goodbye.

phrases.context: A friend asks if you were upset about it — wave it off with a laid-back no.
phrases.notes: 'Jok' = a punchy, casual 'nope', warmer than plain 'ne'. 'Jok' came in from Turkish.

phrases.context: You've got news or a joke and you grab your friend's attention before launching in.
phrases.notes: 'Čuj' = listen (imperative of 'čuti'); 'čuj ovo' = 'hear this'. 'Ej' is just an attention-grabber.

phrases.context: Someone keeps doing the forbidden thing just to prove a point — name it for what it is.
phrases.notes: 'Inat' = stubborn defiance, doing a thing precisely because you were told not to. From Turkish; a point of pride.

phrases.context: A friend suggests something you think is a total waste of time — dismiss it as lame.
phrases.notes: Literally 'without connection' — 'bez' (without) forces 'veza' into the genitive 'veze'.

phrases.context: Your friend finally lands on the exact song you wanted — light up and confirm it.
phrases.notes: Confirms you've nailed the right thing; also used to wrap a conversation or declare something done.

phrases.context: Your friend is hesitating before a bold move — egg him on to go all in.
phrases.notes: Literally 'only strong', from 'jak' (strong). The Serbian 'send it' — pure go-for-it encouragement.
